Sample Size Planning for Power for the Indirect (Mediation) Effect

Source: R/ss_power_indirect_effect.R
ss_power_indirect_effect.Rd

Power, or the sample size required for a desired power, for the test of the indirect effect \(a b\) in the simple mediation model, with paths specified in standardized metric (unit-variance \(X\), \(M\), and \(Y\)). The default test is joint significance (the indirect effect is declared when both \(\hat a\) and \(\hat b\) are individually significant), which tracks the resampling tests' power closely and far exceeds the Sobel test in small samples (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007); the Sobel normal-theory test is available for comparison. Power comes from the exact sampling distribution of the two path t statistics, with \(X\) random by default. This is the power counterpart of the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) planner ss_aipe_indirect_effect, and the planning complement of the analysis function mediate.

Usage

ss_power_indirect_effect(
  true_std_reg_coef_a,
  true_std_reg_coef_b,
  true_std_reg_coef_direct = 0,
  desired_power = NULL,
  specified_N = NULL,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  method = c("joint_significance", "sobel"),
  random_predictors = TRUE
)

Arguments

true_std_reg_coef_a

Population standardized regression coefficient of the \(X \to M\) path \(a\).

true_std_reg_coef_b

Population standardized regression coefficient of the \(M \to Y\) path \(b\), holding \(X\).

true_std_reg_coef_direct

Population standardized regression coefficient of the direct effect \(c'\) of \(X\) on \(Y\) holding \(M\). Defaults to 0; it enters only through the residual variance of \(Y\).

desired_power

Desired power; supply this to solve for \(N\).

specified_N

Total sample size \(N\); supply this to evaluate the realized power. Specify exactly one of desired_power and specified_N.

alpha_level

Two-sided Type I error rate for each component test. Defaults to 0.05.

method

"joint_significance" (default) or "sobel".

random_predictors

TRUE (default) when \(X\) is random, as when it is measured, and FALSE when it is fixed by design, as when groups are assigned. The mediator is random under either setting.

Value

A tidy data.frame with necessary_N (or specified_N), power_ab (the power to detect the indirect effect \(a b\), the quantity the sample size is planned against), the powers of the tests of the two paths (power_a, power_b; NA for the Sobel method), the paths (true_std_reg_coef_a, true_std_reg_coef_b, true_std_reg_coef_direct), their implied standardized indirect effect true_std_indirect_effect, and alpha_level. The method is recorded in the "method" attribute and the predictor model in the "random_predictors" attribute. The result carries the dmar_ss_power class, so tidy reports the sample size and the power to detect the indirect effect (the row power_ab), and glance adds the component powers and the planning inputs.

Details

With unit-variance variables, \(M = a X + e_M\) and \(Y = c' X + b M + e_Y\), with normal errors of variances \(1 - a^2\) and \(\sigma^2_{e_Y} = 1 - (b^2 + c'^2 + 2 a b c')\), which must be positive, or the function stops. As in mediate, \(t_a\) tests the slope of \(M\) on \(X\) (\(N - 2\) degrees of freedom) and \(t_b\) the coefficient of \(M\) in the regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) and \(M\) (\(N - 3\)). Given \(X\), \(t_a\) is noncentral t with noncentrality \(a \sqrt{SS_X / (1 - a^2)}\); given \(X\) and \(M\), \(t_b\) is noncentral t with noncentrality \(b \sqrt{SS_{M \cdot X}} / \sigma_{e_Y}\), where \(SS_{M \cdot X}\) is the residual sum of squares of \(M\) on \(X\). \(SS_{M \cdot X} / (1 - a^2)\) is chi square on \(N - 2\) degrees of freedom in every design, because \(M\) is random given \(X\); \(SS_X\) is chi square on \(N - 1\) with \(X\) random, and \(N\) with \(X\) fixed at variance 1 (divisor \(N\); two groups of equal size, for example). Each power averages the noncentral t power over these chi squares, by Gauss-Hermite sums on their normal scores.

\(SS_{M \cdot X}\) is the error sum of squares of one test and the predictor sum of squares of the other, so the tests are dependent: power_ab is the probability that both reject, which is below power_a times power_b. The first-order Sobel statistic of mediate equals \(t_a t_b / \sqrt{t_a^2 + t_b^2}\), and its power is the probability, integrated numerically, that it exceeds the normal critical value; power_a and power_b are then NA. Because it refers t statistics to the normal, its power need not rise with \(N\): with paths of .9 and .05 it falls from .0729 at \(N = 10\) to .0562 at 59, and with paths of .8 and .02 and alpha_level = .5 it is .5072 at 12 and .5035 at 59, and does not reach .507 again until 216. The joint significance power rose with \(N\) in each of 1,000 settings checked at every \(N\) from 10 to 1,500 (paths from .001 to .99 in absolute value, alpha_level from .0001 to .997, \(X\) random or fixed), which is not a proof. So the search assumes neither: necessary_N is the smallest \(N\) of at least 10 whose power reaches desired_power. It scans upward, passing over a range of \(N\) only where a bound shows that none reaches it: written as its quantile at a fixed normal score, each chi square rises with \(N\), so the power at every \(N\) of the range is at most the power with the noncentralities at the top of the range and each test's threshold (critical value times scale) at its least over the range. Where a path is near zero, the power is also at most the rate at which the test of that path rejects when the path is zero plus \(\phi(1)\) (the standard normal density at 1) times the expected square of its noncentrality (for the Sobel method, the test of \(|t|\) against the normal critical value, since the Sobel statistic is at most the smaller of \(|t_a|\) and \(|t_b|\)), which lets the search pass at once over a long range in which the power stays just below desired_power. It stops at \(N\) = 10,000,000 with an error of class dmar_computation_failed. The tests check power_ab against raw-data simulation within Monte Carlo error at the plan for power .80 and at one case fewer.

Fixing each noncentrality at its population standard error and multiplying the two powers overstates the joint significance power: with paths of .39 that approximation gives .8017 at \(N = 65\), where the power is .7675, and the plan for .80 is 69.

References

Fritz, M. S., & MacKinnon, D. P. (2007). Required sample size to detect the mediated effect. Psychological Science, 18(3), 233–239. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01882.x

MacKinnon, D. P., Lockwood, C. M., Hoffman, J. M., West, S. G., & Sheets, V. (2002). A comparison of methods to test mediation and other intervening variable effects. Psychological Methods, 7(1), 83–104. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.7.1.83

See also

mediate to analyze the study this plans; ss_aipe_indirect_effect to plan for confidence interval width instead of detection; design_consequences for what the chosen design delivers.

Examples

# Fritz and MacKinnon's (2007) running scenario (a = b = .39), X random.
ss_power_indirect_effect(true_std_reg_coef_a = .39,
                         true_std_reg_coef_b = .39, desired_power = .80)
#>  term                     value
#>  necessary_N              69   
#>  power_ab                 0.801
#>  power_a                  0.921
#>  power_b                  0.871
#>  true_std_reg_coef_a      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_b      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_direct 0    
#>  true_std_indirect_effect 0.152
#>  alpha_level              0.050

# X fixed by design (two groups of equal size); the mediator is random.
ss_power_indirect_effect(true_std_reg_coef_a = .39,
                         true_std_reg_coef_b = .39, desired_power = .80,
                         random_predictors = FALSE)
#>  term                     value
#>  necessary_N              68   
#>  power_ab                 0.805
#>  power_a                  0.931
#>  power_b                  0.866
#>  true_std_reg_coef_a      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_b      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_direct 0    
#>  true_std_indirect_effect 0.152
#>  alpha_level              0.050

# A near-zero a path against a larger b: the weak link drives the requirement.
ss_power_indirect_effect(true_std_reg_coef_a = .14,
                         true_std_reg_coef_b = .39, desired_power = .80)
#>  term                     value
#>  necessary_N              398  
#>  power_ab                 0.801
#>  power_a                  0.801
#>  power_b                  1.000
#>  true_std_reg_coef_a      0.140
#>  true_std_reg_coef_b      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_direct 0    
#>  true_std_indirect_effect 0.055
#>  alpha_level              0.050

# Realized power at a given N, and the Sobel test at the same N.
ss_power_indirect_effect(true_std_reg_coef_a = .39,
                         true_std_reg_coef_b = .39, specified_N = 75)
#>  term                     value
#>  specified_N              75   
#>  power_ab                 0.844
#>  power_a                  0.940
#>  power_b                  0.898
#>  true_std_reg_coef_a      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_b      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_direct 0    
#>  true_std_indirect_effect 0.152
#>  alpha_level              0.050
ss_power_indirect_effect(true_std_reg_coef_a = .39,
                         true_std_reg_coef_b = .39, specified_N = 75,
                         method = "sobel")
#>  term                     value
#>  specified_N              75   
#>  power_ab                 0.727
#>  power_a                  <NA> 
#>  power_b                  <NA> 
#>  true_std_reg_coef_a      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_b      0.390
#>  true_std_reg_coef_direct 0    
#>  true_std_indirect_effect 0.152
#>  alpha_level              0.050
